sum: Imperial Brands (LON: IMB) shares closed 13.3% higher today after Altria confirmed it is considering a possible cash offer for the Bristol-based maker of Lambert & Butler and Golden Virginia. Altria, the US group behind Marlboro, is also talking to a third party about taking part of the business.

The shares ended the session at 3,432p, up 402p from 3,030p at yesterday’s close, after touching 3,562p during the day. They have climbed since the start of October, when they stood at 2,424p, and the group is now valued at about £26bn.

Altria issued its statement under Rule 2.4 of the Takeover Code, a notice that a possible bid is being considered, at 12.56pm. It said any offer, if made, is likely to be solely in cash, and that there can be no certainty an offer will be made or on what terms. Deutsche Bank and Perella Weinberg are Altria’s financial advisers.

The statement confirmed press speculation that had already lifted the shares earlier in the session. Bloomberg reported that Japan Tobacco, the Tokyo-based group behind Camel outside the US, is studying a deal. Altria’s statement does not name its third party, but the Telegraph reported that Altria has partnered with Japan Tobacco.
Altria has disclosed no price, so there is no offer to measure the share price against. The move reflects the prospect of a bid, not its terms.
The approach also lands in the UK’s debate over companies leaving London. Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, commented:
This departure would be a £26bn blow to the FTSE 100 and the second loss in just one week.

Can MO's Basic Brand Benefit From Growing Discount Cigarette Demand?
sum: Altria Group, Inc. MO is gaining traction in the discount cigarette market through the Basic brand, as continued economic pressures push adult smokers toward lower-priced options. The brand's growing retail presence reflects Altria's focus on offering competitive products in stores where discount cigarettes are particularly relevant.

The discount segment accounted for 34.1% of total cigarette retail sales in the third quarter of 2026, up 2 percentage points year over year and 0.3 percentage points sequentially. Management attributed the shift toward discount cigarettes primarily to continued pressure on adult smokers' discretionary income amid elevated household expenses.

Basic has gained retail share amid this shift toward discount cigarettes. The brand's retail share reached 3.2% in the third quarter of 2026, compared with 1.4% a year earlier, representing an increase of 1.8 percentage points. Basic's retail share also improved 0.3 percentage points from the preceding quarter, highlighting Basic's continued momentum within the discount category.

The broader discount market also shows a clear shift in purchasing patterns. Branded discount cigarettes represented 18.1% of total cigarette retail sales, up from 16.7% a year earlier. Deep-discount products accounted for another 16%, compared with 15.4% in the prior-year quarter.

Basic's continued retail share gains strengthen Altria's positioning in the discount cigarette segment. Sustained pressure on household budgets remains an important factor influencing demand for lower-priced cigarette options.

Altria’s shares have gained 9.3% over the past three months, outperforming the industry’s 0.3% decline. The stock has also outperformed peers Philip Morris International PM and Turning Point Brands, Inc. TPB, whose shares have declined 3.9% and 44.5%, respectively, during the same period.

From a valuation standpoint, MO trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 12.76X, down from the industry’s average of 15.29X. The company is also trading at a discount to Philip Morris (with a forward price-to-sales ratio of 20.56X) and Turning Point Brands (20.39X).

sum: One issue that new investors often grapple with is whether to buy stocks with small amounts of capital or wait until they have more substantial cash to enter the game.

Hint: Starting small is better than waiting or not starting at all. Some experts call it micro-investing, but whatever the label, prospective market participants, particularly those with the luxury of time on their side, are best served by starting with small stakes and putting the advantages of compounding and long-term horizons to work.
Just $5,000 is a great starting point for harnessing income from Altria stock. Image source: Getty Images.
With that in mind, the example of starting somewhat small with reliable dividend growth stocks, including tobacco behemoth Altria (MO +0.25%), is worth examining.
To be fair, $5,000 isn't a small amount of money, but it's not enough to retire on, either. However, it is a solid starting point for investors seeking a fair amount of income from Altria.

Here are the particulars on $5,000 worth of Altria shares. This Dividend King, or one of the companies with a dividend increase of at least 50 consecutive years, yields 5.8%, as of Thursday, Nov. 19. That's nearly 80 basis points above the yield on 10-year Treasuries. Based on the tobacco stock's closing price of $74.68 on Nov. 19, $5,000 buys 67 shares (I slightly rounded up there). Factor in the $4.44 per share annual dividend, and a $5,000 stake in Altria today generates nearly $297.50 in annual income.

That's not too shabby. Call it $300 and Altria's dividend, assuming it's not being reinvested, could cover a couple of months of phone bills or a nice dinner out. On the other hand, $300 isn't an earth-shattering amount of money, suggesting that investors should maintain perspective on Altria's income-generating capabilities.

Why do falling cigarette volumes matter so much to the model?

Cigarette consumption in the United States has declined for decades, driven by health awareness, higher taxes, indoor smoking restrictions and the rise of alternatives. Industry volume declines have often been described in the mid-single-digit range annually, with swings in some years tied to inflation, illicit trade and the availability of cheap disposable vapes. A declining-volume business works only if price increases and cost control more than make up the difference in earnings. The strategy is mathematically sound while consumers accept higher prices, but it becomes harder when household budgets are stretched and smokers shift toward discount brands or other forms of nicotine. The trade-down dynamic is visible in the market share data. Marlboro maintains a leading position in premium cigarettes, yet value-priced competitors have advanced ground when the gap between premium and discount shelf prices widened.

Tobacco is among the most heavily regulated consumer categories. The Food and Drug Administration has authority over product standards, marketing and premarket authorization. Nicotine content standards, flavor restrictions on non-combustible products and state-level bans are additional areas where rules can change quickly.
